n: During a public reading of the law, the people find a command that Ammonites and Moabites may not join the assembly of Israel. This chapter may describe events some years after the wall’s dedication.

f.w: in the audience of the people
f.g: In the hearing of the people.

f.w: should not come into the congregation of God for ever

n: The reason: centuries earlier these nations refused Israel food and water and hired the prophet Balaam to curse them. But God turned the curse into a blessing.

f.w: turned the curse into a blessing

n: The people separate from those of foreign descent who had mixed in without committing to the covenant. Notably, Ruth the Moabite was welcomed long before because she fully embraced Israel’s God (Ruth 1:16).
A scandal: Eliashib, the priest in charge of the temple storerooms, had formed an alliance with Tobiah — Nehemiah’s old Ammonite enemy.

f.g: Related by marriage or bound by alliance (compare Nehemiah 6:18).

n: He gave Tobiah a large room in the temple courts — a storeroom meant for offerings and tithes that supported the Levites and priests. An enemy of God’s work now had an apartment in God’s house.

f.g: Grain offerings; “meat” means food.
A fragrant resin burned as incense.

n: This happened while Nehemiah was away. After twelve years as governor, he returned to the Persian king’s court in 433 BC, then later got permission to come back.

f.g: Persian kings also held the title “king of Babylon.”

n: Back in Jerusalem, Nehemiah learns what Eliashib had done for Tobiah.

f.g: Learned of the wrong.

n: Deeply upset, Nehemiah throws all of Tobiah’s furniture out of the room — a dramatic act of cleansing the temple, a little like Jesus driving out the moneychangers.

f.w: I cast forth all the household stuff

n: He orders the rooms purified and restores the sacred vessels and offerings to their proper place.
The Levites and singers had not been receiving their share of tithes, so they had left temple service to go farm their own fields to survive.

f.g: Their assigned share of tithes and offerings.

f.w: fled every one to his field

n: Nehemiah confronts the leaders: “Why is the house of God forsaken?” — echoing their own covenant promise not to forsake it. He brings the Levites back to their posts.

f.w: Why is the house of God forsaken?

f.g: Argued, rebuked.

n: The people resume paying tithes of grain, wine, and oil. Faithful tithing kept temple service running.
He appoints a trustworthy committee — a priest, a scribe, a Levite, and an assistant — to manage the storehouses and distribute fairly. Faithfulness was the main qualification.
Nehemiah prays again: remember my good deeds for your house. His short prayers show a man who constantly worked with God in mind.

f.w: wipe not out my good deeds

n: Nehemiah sees people working and trading on the Sabbath — pressing grapes, loading donkeys, and bringing goods to sell in Jerusalem. He warns them.

f.g: Crushing grapes by foot — farm labor forbidden on the Sabbath.
Loading.

n: Merchants from Tyre, a Phoenician port city, were selling fish and goods to Jews on the Sabbath.

f.g: Phoenician traders from the coast of what is now Lebanon.

n: Nehemiah rebukes the nobles, who were responsible for allowing it: Why are you making the Sabbath unholy?

f.g: To treat something holy as ordinary.

n: He reminds them that Sabbath-breaking was one reason their ancestors suffered exile. Repeating the sin would bring more trouble.
Nehemiah takes practical action: the gates close at sunset Friday as the Sabbath begins and stay shut until it ends, with guards to stop any goods coming in.

f.w: began to be dark before the sabbath
f.g: The Sabbath began at sunset on Friday evening.

n: Some merchants camp outside the walls once or twice, hoping to tempt buyers to come out.

f.g: Camped outside the city.

n: Nehemiah warns them sternly that he will use force if they come again. They stop coming. Firm leadership protected the Sabbath.

f.w: I will lay hands on you
f.g: I will arrest you or use force.

n: He assigns purified Levites to guard the gates and keep the day holy, then prays for mercy. Nehemiah asks not just for reward but for God’s mercy — he knows he needs it too.

f.w: spare me according to the greatness of thy mercy

n: Another old problem returns: Jewish men marrying women from Ashdod, Ammon, and Moab — breaking the covenant they had signed.

f.w: married wives of Ashdod, of Ammon, and of Moab

n: Half their children can’t even speak Hebrew. Losing the language meant losing access to the scriptures and to Israel’s identity — a concern similar to Lehi’s reason for obtaining the brass plates.

f.w: could not speak in the Jews' language
f.g: They spoke the language of their mothers’ peoples, not Hebrew.

n: Nehemiah reacts with fierce anger — rebuking, striking some, and pulling out their hair as a sign of public disgrace — and makes them swear not to arrange such marriages. His methods reflect his time and his passion for the covenant.

f.g: A humiliating public punishment; compare Ezra, who pulled out his own hair in grief (Ezra 9:3).

n: He points to Solomon: no king was greater or more loved by God, yet his foreign wives turned his heart to idols. If Solomon could fall, so could they.

f.w: Did not Solomon king of Israel sin by these things?

f.g: Foreign women.

n: Should the rest of us follow your example and betray God too? Nehemiah frames it as a matter of loyalty to the covenant.

f.g: Foreign wives who did not worship Israel’s God.

n: Worst of all, a grandson of the high priest had married the daughter of Sanballat, Nehemiah’s chief enemy. Nehemiah drives him away.

f.g: Expelled him from Jerusalem and from priestly service.

n: Nehemiah asks God to remember those who defiled the priesthood and the sacred covenant tied to it.
He purifies the community from foreign religious influence and reorganizes the priests and Levites so each has a clear assignment.

f.g: Duties, shifts of service.

n: He arranges for the firewood and firstfruit offerings to be brought on schedule. The book ends with his simple, repeated prayer: “Remember me, O my God, for good.” Nehemiah’s legacy is faithful, persistent effort for the Lord’s house.

f.w: Remember me, O my God, for good
